questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the chief defect of the first national charter.
questions.stem: A city planner's memo asks the council to explain why a national charter adopted in 1781 had failed within five years, and lists three candidate causes. Which cause was the most serious?

options.text: It denied the central government any power to tax individuals, so it depended on state requests
It set up a permanent national court that could enforce its own judgments
options.misconception: Believes a national judiciary existed; there was none

options.text: It required unanimous consent of all thirteen states for ordinary legislative business
options.misconception: Confuses the nine-state rule with a unanimity rule

options.text: It let the national congress amend the charter without any action by the states
options.misconception: Believes congress alone could amend the charter

questions.explanation: Without taxing power the centre could not fund itself or pay war debts, so it depended on state contributions, which is why reform came so quickly. It also had no national court to enforce anything.
questions.hint: Look for the power the centre never had.

options.misconception: Miscounts the mid-sized state at the rounding step

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why opponents resisted the new charter and what they won.
questions.stem: The minutes of a state ratifying convention in 1788 record that delegates approved the new constitution but insisted on further safeguards before the vote. Explain in a few sentences why a sizeable group opposed ratification and what their pressure achieved.

answer.exemplar: Opponents doubted that a stronger national government would not repeat the abuses of the British government they had just fought to end, and they feared that a large national government could itself become the danger rather than the remedy. They also distrusted a charter that said almost nothing about the rights of individuals. Their leverage came from ratifying conventions rather than legislatures, where approval was given conditionally, and the campaign for the promised safeguards ended with ten amendments added to the constitution in 1791.

questions.explanation: Opponents feared concentrated national power and wanted explicit protections before approving the charter. By making approval conditional in state conventions, they forced the amendments of 1789 and 1791.
questions.hint: They traded approval for written guarantees.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a 1786 meeting was called and why it failed.
questions.stem: A contractor asked the city engineer to explain, for a public meeting, why a small meeting of delegates in 1786 was convened to fix the national charter and why it did not fix it. Answer in a short paragraph.

answer.exemplar: The national congress, unable to tax, fund the war debt, or settle disputes between states, called for a meeting in Annapolis to devise amendments to the confederation, and it invited every state to send delegates. Only a handful of states attended, partly through poor roads and partly because the states that had already seen the conference fail in 1785 refused to send anyone, and no amendment could be adopted without the consent of nine states. The result was a resolution calling for a fuller convention, which is what brought the delegates together at Philadelphia the following year with a mandate to write a new constitution rather than patch the old one.

questions.explanation: The meeting was meant to amend a charter that could not fund itself, and too few states attended for anything to be done. Its only result was the call for a convention with wider authority.
questions.hint: Count the states that had to agree to anything.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the trade clause and the counting clause were linked.
questions.stem: The state enabling act contains a clause on port inspections, and the planner wants the history behind it recorded. In a short paragraph, explain why the framers agreed both to count enslaved people at three fifths for representation and to protect the foreign trade until 1808.

answer.exemplar: The counting rule and the trade clause answered the same set of complaints in opposite ways. Southern states wanted a larger share of representation and a stronger claim that the trade in enslaved people was a commercial interest protected like any other, and they had leverage because without an agreement the northern states could have written the constitution without them. Northern states wanted the slave trade ended quickly, and the bargain gave them the three fifths rule in exchange for a twenty-year protection of the trade, which did expire under the terms of the act approved in 1808.

questions.explanation: The two clauses were the paired terms of a bargain in which each side conceded on one point and held on the other. Southern states gained representation weight, and the trade protection carried a fixed end date.
questions.hint: They were two halves of one bargain.

answer.exemplar: The opponents doubted that a stronger national government would not repeat the abuses of the British government they had just fought to end, and they feared that a large national government might become the danger rather than the remedy, especially without a written list of individual protections. questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the structural cause of the confederation's failure.
questions.stem: The 1787 constitutional convention's own record is quoted on the council wall, and a citizen asks why the earlier arrangement could not be patched. Explain the structural problem in a short paragraph.

answer.exemplar: The earlier arrangement was a treaty among sovereign states rather than a government over individuals, so its centre could only ask the states for money, troops, and obedience, and the states were free to refuse. It also had no executive to carry out its own decisions, no national court to enforce them, and no power to regulate commerce or settle the disputes between states that were multiplying as the country expanded. Worse, the rules for amending it required the consent of every state, so the very weakness that needed correcting was built into the process of correcting it, and the only way out was for the states to agree among themselves to hand a convention the authority to write something different.

questions.explanation: The centre could only request what the states might refuse, and had no executive, court, or commerce power to make requests stick. Amending the charter needed every state, so a new text was needed.
questions.hint: Think about who obeyed the centre, and how it was fixed.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the significance of equal state representation in the upper chamber.
questions.stem: The appraisal for the courthouse block must record why small states accepted the new bargain. In a short paragraph, explain what equal representation of states in the upper chamber accomplished in the 1787 settlement.

answer.exemplar: The equality of states in the upper chamber was what made the settlement possible, because small states had concluded that pure representation by population would reduce them to a permanent minority in a government they were being asked to join, and some had already refused to send delegates to an earlier meeting for that reason. At the same time, giving that equality a price in the other chamber, where seats followed population and therefore favoured the large states, allowed the large states to accept the bargain in turn. The result was a structure in which neither side could be outvoted simply by size, and in which the consent of a state remained necessary for the most consequential measures, which is why the new upper chamber later proved to be a check on the power of the more populous chamber.

questions.explanation: Equal state votes in the upper chamber reassured small states that population could not outvote them, and the price was paid in the lower chamber. A state's senators also became a real check.
questions.hint: Ask what the small states were protected against.

answer.exemplar: A narrow margin in a state that had actively debated the charter shows that the new constitution was adopted, but not by a body persuaded of its merits, and that approval was secured by a coalition rather than by an agreement about what the document should contain. Because the arguments of the opponents remained unanswered in public, the demand for a written declaration of rights survived the ratification and was carried forward into the first session of the new congress, where the ten amendments were proposed. options.text: Six thousand six hundred, but only because the free number is added twice
options.misconception: Gets the total right for the wrong reason

questions.explanation: Three fifths of 2,000 is 1,200, and 5,400 free persons plus 1,200 gives a base of 6,600. The fraction applies to the number returned as enslaved, not to the free population.
questions.hint: Apply the fraction to the enslaved column.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of the great compromise.
questions.stem: The agreement reached in 1787 is described in the exhibit text, and the planner asks what the bargain did not settle. In a short paragraph, explain the main limitation of the settlement on representation.

answer.exemplar: The settlement ended the immediate argument between small and large states over the shape of the legislature, but it did so by accepting the reality of the population count rather than by questioning it, and the count itself was built on a rule that treated enslaved people as three fifths of a person and a further rule that protected the trade in them until 1808. For more than two decades after that, the arithmetic of representation and the compromises that sustained it became the sharpest point of conflict in the country, and the bargain that satisfied both sections in 1787 proved to be one of the things that the country was soon divided over. The limitation of the compromise was therefore not technical but constitutional, since it fixed a principle about who counted rather than leaving that question to later argument.

questions.explanation: The bargain settled the shape of the legislature but built it on a count that excluded most enslaved people from full count. That arithmetic became the sharpest constitutional conflict of the next decades.
questions.hint: Look at the population rule underneath the seats.

questions.learningObjective: Determine which pair of claims about state ratification is accurate.
questions.stem: Voters in the conventions asked the clerk how the charter became binding. Which pair of statements about the ratification is entirely accurate?

options.text: Nine states were required, and approval was given by conventions or legislatures as each state chose
Thirteen states were required, and approval was given by a single national convention
options.misconception: Confuses the threshold with a national ratifying body

options.text: Nine states were required, and approval was given only by elected legislatures
options.misconception: Believes only legislatures could ratify

options.text: Thirteen states were required, and each state needed a two-thirds majority to approve
options.misconception: Invents a two-thirds state requirement

questions.explanation: Nine of the thirteen states had to approve, and each state chose a convention or a legislature as it preferred. There was no single national ratifying body, and a two-thirds state threshold never existed.
questions.hint: Nine states, and the choice belonged to each state.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the historical significance of the founding-era crisis.
questions.stem: The weakness of the earlier charter is the subject of the closing exhibit panel. In a short paragraph, explain why the crisis of the 1780s mattered beyond the founding period itself.

answer.exemplar: The crisis mattered because the answer to it, a constitution that divided power between a national government and the states and that made the national authority operate directly on individuals, became the template for later state constitutions in the revolutions of the following decades, where American constitutions and bills of rights were widely copied, and the amendments of 1791 gave the world a written statement of individual rights that other movements could cite. It also settled the question of what a constitution was for, namely to fix the terms on which power is granted rather than to leave it to custom, and that idea travelled with the written constitutions themselves. Finally, the crisis left a durable settlement between national authority and state sovereignty, a settlement that would be contested legally and politically for the next century and a half.

questions.explanation: The crisis produced a written constitution, a written list of rights, and a durable division of national and state authority. Those exports were copied far beyond their country, and the settlement stayed open to contest.
questions.hint: Follow the settlement's effects beyond the founding.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Analyze a record of the deal struck on representation.

stimulus.body: We were called together to do one thing, and that thing was to form a constitution that should be the framework of a government for a great country. The complaints against the old confederation were general and acknowledged; the evil to be cured was the want of power in the centre, and the difficulty was how to give that power without extinguishing the states. The compromise which satisfied the members from the small states in the one branch and the members from the large states in the other was, in my judgment, the masterstroke of the whole plan.

questions.stem: A published debate quoted in the council file describes the bargain as its author understood it. Which reading is most faithful to the passage?

options.text: The bargain gave the national centre enough power to act while leaving the states meaningful in the legislature
The bargain preserved the old system almost exactly, with only a small increase in national power
options.misconception: Reads the outcome as continuity with the confederation

options.text: The bargain gave the national government unrestricted power and left the states as mere subdivisions
options.misconception: Overstates how much the bargain centralised power

options.text: The bargain was reached by a single vote, with no serious disagreement beforehand
options.misconception: Invents a unanimous agreement at the outset

questions.explanation: The speaker treats the bargain as the cure for a centre that lacked power, achieved without extinguishing the states, which is the two-chamber arrangement. The passage claims neither continuity with the old system nor unlimited national power.
questions.hint: He names both a gain and a limit.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose the effect of conditional approval on the new charter.

stimulus.body: We approve the constitution, upon the express condition that the first congress, immediately after its meeting, shall propose amendments to it, to be ratified by the legislatures of the several states. Until those amendments are ratified, this declaration shall be considered as a part of the constitution and as binding upon the people of this state.

questions.stem: The briefing given to the council quotes a state's conditional approval. What did conditional approval make possible?

options.text: The state approved the charter while insisting that written protections be added before it felt secure
A legal basis for the new government to be delayed until the amendments were ratified
options.misconception: Infers a legal delay of the government

options.text: A reason for the state to withdraw from the union once the amendments were ratified
options.misconception: Invents a right of withdrawal

options.text: A power for the state legislature to declare the original constitution void
options.misconception: Reads a condition as a power to void the charter

questions.explanation: By approving with an express condition attached, the state joined the new system and made written protections part of the bargain, which is how the amendments were produced. It did not suspend the government.
questions.hint: Read the condition as a demand, not a veto.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the practical effect of equal state representation.
questions.stem: The subdivision proposal for the estate adds a chamber that must approve any change to the regional plan. Which founding-era arrangement makes that chamber's consent a genuine check rather than a formality?

options.text: The upper chamber gave every state an equal vote, so no state could be outvoted by sheer size
The lower chamber gave every state an equal vote, so all states held the same leverage
options.misconception: Assigns equal state votes to the wrong chamber

options.text: The states could amend the constitution by their own votes, so the chamber's consent was optional
options.misconception: Confuses amendment by the states with chamber approval

options.misconception: Confuses ratification with the powers of the congress

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a ratification tally as a state-by-state outcome.
questions.stem: Counting the votes across the states, the planner records that four states approved in the first wave, three more followed over the next year, and the remaining states waited until the end, with the last approval arriving in 1790. What does the pattern show?

options.text: Ratification was a state-by-state contest spread over years, ending only when the threshold was met
The charter was defeated in the early waves and rescued by a later procedural change
options.misconception: Reads early approvals as defeats

options.text: The states voted as blocs, so the count in each wave was identical across them
options.misconception: Invented uniform voting blocs

options.text: The nine-state threshold was raised once the early waves showed weakness
options.misconception: Invents a change to the ratification threshold

questions.explanation: The spread across four waves shows that each state decided on its own timetable, and the process ended when the ninth approval made the charter binding, with the last state trailing in 1790. Nothing indicates defeat.
questions.hint: Each state moved when it was ready.
